title: Light, Timing, Sleep
outcomeStatement: By the end of this, your days will start and end at times your body agrees with.
careNote: Behavioural protocols only. Nothing here is medical advice. If your sleep problems are persistent or severe, that's a conversation for a doctor, not an app.

practices.title: Your actual times, honestly
practices.body: Write down, as best you can remember, what time you got into bed and what time you got up each day this past week. Not your intended times. The real ones.

practices.title: Light first, everything else after
practices.body: Morning outdoor light is the strongest available signal for setting your body clock — and it sets tonight's sleep, not this morning's alertness. Overcast still counts; through a window doesn't.

practices.title: Audit your evening light
practices.body: Walk your home after 9pm and list every light source that's on — overhead bulbs, screens, the bright kitchen. Write which ones you could dim or turn off without much loss.

practices.title: What do you stay up for?
practices.body: Be honest about what those late hours give you that the rest of the day doesn't.

practices.title: One fixed wake time
practices.body: Choose a single wake time you can hold seven days a week, including weekends, and write why it's realistic. A consistent wake time does more for sleep quality than a consistent bedtime.

practices.title: The first yawn
practices.body: Tonight, notice when you first genuinely feel sleepy — and what you do next. Most people get one clear invitation and then override it. Just mark when it arrives.
practices.noticeFor: the first real wave of sleepiness

practices.title: Delay the first coffee
practices.body: Tomorrow, push your first caffeine 90 minutes past waking. Write the time you'll have it, and set a reminder if you need one. Then note how the afternoon feels compared to usual.

practices.title: Colder and darker
practices.body: Make one change to bring the bedroom temperature down and one to make it darker — a cracked window, a thinner duvet, a blackout curtain, tape over the standby light. Body temperature has to drop for sleep to start.

practices.title: Twenty minutes of deliberate rest
practices.body: Some time this afternoon, lie down for twenty minutes with a guided non-sleep deep rest or yoga nidra recording. Not a nap — you stay awake. Write how you felt afterwards.

practices.title: What does a good day after a bad night look like?
practices.body: One bad night is normal and survivable. What do you need to stop expecting of yourself on those days?

practices.cue: After a fixed hour you choose this evening
practices.behavior: no bright overhead lights — lamps only
practices.title: Overheads off
practices.body: Bright light late in the evening pushes your clock later. Low, warm, and below eye level is the whole rule.

practices.title: Write your wind-down
practices.body: Design a twenty-minute sequence you'll run before bed — three steps, same order every night, no screens in it. Write the three steps down. The consistency is what signals the body, not the content.

practices.title: Tired decisions
practices.body: Today, notice the choices you make after 10pm and how they differ from the ones you'd make at 10am. Same person, different judgement. Just count the ones you'd have made differently.
practices.noticeFor: a decision you'd make differently rested

practices.title: Two weeks ago you wrote your real times. What moved?
practices.body: Read day 1 first. Then: what actually changed, what didn't, and which single thing is worth keeping past today?
